title: Trump Banner Hung on DOJ Headquarters as White House Grip on Justice Deepens
description_short: Trump Banner Hung on DOJ Headquarters as White House Grip on Justice Deepens
description_medium: A banner bearing President Trump’s face and the slogan “Make America Safe Again” was displayed on the Justice Department headquarters in February 2026. The unusual placement drew attention because the department has a tradition of independence from the White House. The Associated Press reported on the display; its symbolic meaning is a matter of public concern, not a formal change in DOJ authority.
description_long: A large banner featuring Donald Trump’s face has been hung on the exterior of Justice Department headquarters in a physical display of the Republican president’s efforts to exert power over the law enforcement agency. While Trump banners have been hung outside other agencies across Washington, the decision to place one on the storied Justice Department building Thursday amounts to a striking symbol of the erosion of the department’s tradition of independence from White House control. The banner, hung between two columns on one corner of the building, says, “Make America Safe Again,” a slogan used by the administration to tout its efforts to clamp down on illegal immigration and violent crime. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: Trump Casts Doubt on NATO Article 5 Mutual Defense Commitment
description_short: Trump Casts Doubt on NATO Article 5 Mutual Defense Commitment
description_medium: On June 24, 2025, Trump declined to give an unequivocal reaffirmation of NATO’s Article 5 mutual-defense commitment while traveling to the Hague summit. Asked whether the United States would honor the pledge, he said he was committed to “saving lives” and that the answer depended on its definition. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sought to reassure allies.
description_long: On June 24, 2025, en route to a NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands, President Trump publicly cast doubt on the United States' commitment to mutual defense under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. When reporters aboard Air Force One pressed Trump on whether he remained committed to Article 5 — the cornerstone provision holding that an attack on one ally constitutes an attack on all — Trump responded: I'm committed to saving lives. I'm committed to life and safety. He conspicuously declined to reaffirm Article 5 before European allies convened to signal unity against Russian aggression. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte attempted to contain the damage, saying he had no doubt about US commitment. The Hague summit was specifically designed to deter Russian President Vladimir Putin. Congress had passed legislation in the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act prohibiting Trump from unilaterally withdrawing from the North Atlantic Treaty without a two-thirds Senate vote, reflecting bipartisan concerns about Trump's NATO reliability.

title: National Security Adviser Waltz Fired Over Signalgate, Replaced by Rubio in Dual Role
description_short: National Security Adviser Waltz Fired Over Signalgate, Replaced by Rubio in Dual Role
description_medium: Trump removed National Security Adviser Mike Waltz on May 1, 2025, after the Signal chat controversy and nominated him to be U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio took over as interim national security adviser while retaining the State Department post. The arrangement concentrated two senior foreign-policy roles in one official.
description_long: On May 1, 2025, President Trump removed National Security Adviser Mike Waltz—the Army Green Beret veteran who had accidentally added Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg to the Signal war-plans chat in March—and nominated him to be U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations. In the first major personnel shakeup of Trump's second term, Trump named Secretary of State Marco Rubio as interim National Security Adviser while Rubio continued to lead the State Department, a historically unprecedented arrangement that concentrated two major national security roles in one person. Rubio would hold both positions simultaneously, eliminating the formal separation between the nation's top diplomat and its principal White House security coordinator. The NSC had already been gutted of dozens of career professionals by that point. Critics warned the arrangement would compromise both the independence of intelligence advice reaching the president and diplomatic policy coordination globally. The dual appointment reflected the administration's broader pattern of consolidating national security functions under political loyalists while dismantling professional institutional infrastructure.

title: DHS Secretary Mullin Threatens States with Investigations Over Voter Roll Compliance
description_short: DHS Secretary Mullin Threatens States with Investigations Over Voter Roll Compliance
description_medium: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned states in July 2026 that they could face investigations or lose federal funds if they did not meet the administration’s election-security demands, including checks against a federal citizenship database. Courts had recently blocked the SAVE database and rejected several voter-roll demands, making the threats legally contested.
description_long: On July 17, 2026 — one day after Trump's primetime election address — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a White House press conference warning that states could lose federal funding or face federal investigations if they failed to comply with the administration's election security demands, including running voter rolls through the SAVE citizenship verification database. Mullin pledged to aggressively monitor public voter lists to pursue voter fraud cases before and after the November election. The threats came as the administration was already losing all 16 court rulings on its voter roll demands and as the SAVE database had just been blocked by a federal judge. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen called the threats likely hollow given the courts had blocked the underlying initiatives, but warned the statements would further doubts about election processes and create headaches for states preparing for November. Mullin's remarks compounded the chilling effect created by the DOJ's July 7 letters threatening criminal charges against election officials.

title: DOJ Civil Rights Division Gutted and Redirected by Dhillon
description_short: DOJ Civil Rights Division Gutted and Redirected by Dhillon
description_medium: Harmeet Dhillon took charge of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division in April 2025 and redirected its work toward enforcing Trump administration priorities. More than 100 division lawyers had left or accepted deferred resignation by late April. The changes included pausing some police-abuse investigations and opening probes into other issues, prompting concern about the division’s traditional civil-rights mission.
description_long: Harmeet Dhillon, a conservative Trump loyalist who had represented the president in 2020 election lawsuits, was sworn in as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division on April 7, 2025, and immediately reoriented the 68-year-old division away from its founding mission of fighting race-based discrimination. By late April, approximately half the division's lawyers — more than 100 attorneys — had departed or accepted the 'deferred resignation program,' in what a senior DOJ attorney described as 'a complete bloodbath.' Dhillon issued memos redirecting the division's sections to enforce Trump executive orders including 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports' and 'Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling,' replacing decades-long civil rights priorities. The division suspended investigations of police abuse and launched probes into whether Los Angeles was violating gun rights and whether universities were tolerating antisemitism. The Federal Coordination and Compliance Section, historically tasked with enforcing Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act, was directed to focus instead on Trump's gender ideology executive orders.

title: Court Suspends Trump-Era ICE Rule Requiring 7-Day Notice for Congressional Visits
description_short: Court Suspends Trump-Era ICE Rule Requiring 7-Day Notice for Congressional Visits
description_medium: A federal judge temporarily suspended a Department of Homeland Security rule requiring lawmakers to give seven days’ notice before visiting immigration detention sites. Judge Jia Cobb said Democratic members of Congress were likely to show the notice requirement was unlawful and that the government had not offered concrete safety reasons. The ruling restored access while the case continued.
description_long: A judge is temporarily suspending the latest version of a Trump administration policy that requires members of Congress to provide a week’s notice before they can visit immigration detention facilities. U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb in Washington ruled Monday a group of Democratic lawmakers is likely to succeed in showing the seven-day notice requirement is illegal. Thirteen House members sued to challenge the Jan. 8 policy issued by Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. The judge says the Republican administration hasn’t cited any “concrete examples of safety issues posed by congressional visits without advanced notice.” Noem secretly reinstated a notice requirement one day after an immigration officer shot and killed a U.S. citizen in Minneapolis. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: Trump Berates Maryland Governor During Potomac Sewage Crisis
description_short: Trump Berates Maryland Governor During Potomac Sewage Crisis
description_medium: Trump publicly blamed Maryland Governor Wes Moore for a sewage spill into the Potomac after a pipe rupture, although the federal government and D.C. water authority had jurisdiction over the damaged pipe. Moore’s office said the EPA missed a state hearing and accused the administration of shirking cleanup duties. The dispute mixed an environmental emergency with federal-state political conflict.
description_long: President Donald Trump is lashing out at Maryland Gov. Wes Moore over what he says is as a lagging response to a January pipe rupture that sent sewage flowing into the Potomac River northwest of Washington. The federal government and a District of Columbia water authority have jurisdiction over the busted pipe. Still, Trump took aim at Moore on social media Monday and said he “cannot allow incompetent Local ‘Leadership’” to turn the Potomac into “a Disaster Zone.” A spokesman for Moore said Environmental Protection Agency officials did not participate in a recent state legislative hearing about the cleanup and said the Trump administration has been broadly “shirking its responsibility” on the repair and cleanup. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: 52 Deaths in ICE Detention: Mortality Rate Highest in 20 Years
description_short: 52 Deaths in ICE Detention: Mortality Rate Highest in 20 Years
description_medium: A Human Rights Watch report said 52 people died in ICE custody between January 2025 and June 2026, with a death rate far above recent administrations. Detention populations also reached record levels as deaths rose. The report and related investigations identified medical staffing and delayed care concerns, including the case of detainee Maksym Chernyak.
description_long: Between January 20, 2025 and June 4, 2026, 52 people died in ICE custody — the highest mortality rate in over two decades and more than double Trump's first term rate, according to a June 2026 Human Rights Watch report titled Dying in Detention. The death rate was nearly four times that of the Biden administration. The Trump administration pushed ICE detention to a record high of 71,000 people by January 2026, up 77% from January 2025, while the annual death rate tripled — a disproportionate increase. In facilities where deaths occurred, populations were on average 242 detainees higher than the 10-year average in the two weeks before each death. Notable cases include Maksym Chernyak, 44, whose detention staff failed to call emergency services for over four and a half hours during a life-threatening emergency. A CNN investigation found many deaths were preventable due to understaffed medical teams, uninterrupted delays in offsite care, and DHS contractor failures. Deaths in 2026 were on track to exceed 2025.

title: The Nunes Memo: Patel's Four Pages That Helped Dismantle Trust in the Mueller Investigation
description_short: The Nunes Memo: Patel's Four Pages That Helped Dismantle Trust in the Mueller Investigation
description_medium: The four-page Nunes memo, released in February 2018, alleged that the FBI concealed the political origins of the Steele dossier in FISA applications. Kash Patel helped draft the memo. The application itself disclosed Democratic funding of the research, undercutting a central claim. A later inspector general report found serious errors in the applications but did not validate the memo’s specific allegations.
description_long: In January 2018, Kash Patel, then a senior aide to House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes, was the primary drafter of the infamous Nunes Memo — a four-page classified document released on February 2, 2018. The memo alleged that FBI and DOJ officials had committed FISA abuses by concealing the political origins of the Steele dossier from surveillance court judges. The central claim — that the applications did not disclose the DNC's funding of the Steele research — was flatly contradicted by the actual FISA application, which contained a lengthy footnote disclosing the politically-motivated origins. The New York Times later reported that many of the flaws Patel claimed turned out to be false or misleading. While DOJ Inspector General Horowitz's 2019 report did find 17 significant errors in the FISA applications, the specific claims in Patel's memo were largely wrong or cherry-picked. The memo nonetheless served its political purpose: galvanizing Trump supporters, delegitimizing the Mueller investigation, and launching Patel's career as a MAGA national security celebrity.

title: Trump Threatens Criminal Prosecution of Election Officials Who Ran 2020 Election
description_short: Trump Threatens Criminal Prosecution of Election Officials Who Ran 2020 Election
description_medium: Trump said in a March 2025 speech that officials who administered the 2020 election should be jailed. His administration also directed Justice Department reviews and task forces focused on election officials and security systems. The rhetoric raised concern that federal investigations could be used to target people who certified results, despite a lack of new evidence supporting Trump’s fraud claims.
description_long: In a March 14, 2025 speech, Trump declared that election officials who administered the 2020 election should go to jail. The Brennan Center for Justice documented that the Trump administration built an infrastructure of DOJ task forces and working groups targeting election officials who had certified 2020 results. Trump signed an executive order directing the DOJ to review the actions of Chris Krebs — whom Trump himself had appointed to lead the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency — because Krebs had publicly stated the 2020 election was secure. By July 2025, the New York Times reported that senior DOJ officials were exploring whether to bring criminal charges against state and local election officials if they did not sufficiently safeguard election computer systems, based not on new evidence but on unsubstantiated fraud claims. Trump also publicly ordered the DOJ to intervene to free convicted election saboteur Tina Peters, calling her an innocent Political Prisoner, signaling that officials who had assisted his election subversion efforts would be protected.

title: DEI Purge Eliminates Federal LGBTQ Workplace Protections
description_short: DEI Purge Eliminates Federal LGBTQ Workplace Protections
description_medium: Trump’s January 2025 orders dismantled federal DEI programs and revoked contractor protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The changes affected federal agencies and more than 100,000 LGBTQ workers employed by federal contractors, according to the supplied account. Employees were also put on leave or faced new reporting policies, prompting comparison to past government purges.
description_long: On January 21, 2025, Trump signed 'Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,' revoking EO 11246 (1965) and EO 13672 (2014), stripping from federal law the protections against employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity that had covered employees of federal contractors and subcontractors. The order abolished the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs' authority to promote diversity or hold contractors accountable for 'affirmative action,' directly affecting over 100,000 LGBTQ employees of federal contractors. Separately, the January 20 EO on 'Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs' terminated all agency DEI offices, equity action plans, and DEI performance requirements within 60 days, and ordered agencies to identify 'the most egregious and discriminatory DEI practitioners' for investigation. Dozens of Education Department employees were placed on administrative leave for attending a DEI training during Trump's first term. Documents obtained by The Washington Post indicated DOGE planned to identify and fire workers 'tied to diversity initiatives through unspecified other means,' extending the purge beyond those in formal DEI roles.

title: Trump Ukraine Peace Plan Favors Russian Territorial Demands
description_short: Trump Ukraine Peace Plan Favors Russian Territorial Demands
description_medium: A draft Ukraine peace plan negotiated by Trump administration envoys and Moscow called for Ukraine to cede occupied territory and limit its military. Ukrainian officials said the terms favored Russia, and the proposal offered no firm U.S. or European obligation to defend Ukraine after a future attack. Trump set a Thanksgiving deadline for Kyiv to respond.
description_long: In November 2025, the Associated Press obtained a draft of Trump's Ukraine peace plan — negotiated between the Trump administration and Moscow by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — which would require Ukraine to cede occupied territories to Russia and limit the size of the Ukrainian military. Ukrainian officials described the proposal as decidedly favorable to Russia, which had started the war through an unprovoked invasion. The plan included a side agreement on security guarantees that explicitly did not obligate the US or European allies to intervene in the event of future Russian aggression against Ukraine. Ukrainian officials told Axios that after a five-hour Kremlin meeting between Witkoff, Kushner, and Putin, the US proposal worsened from Kyiv's perspective, with American envoys seemingly selling Russia's demand for full Donbas annexation. Trump gave Zelensky a Thanksgiving deadline to accept the plan. Zelensky said Ukraine faced an impossible choice between national dignity and losing its primary backer. Trump claimed Zelensky's negotiators love the plan while Russian officials simultaneously registered objections.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Ukraine Peace Plan Favors Russian Territorial Demands
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Ukraine Peace Plan Favors Russian Territorial Demands
preserved_fields.description_long: In November 2025, the Associated Press obtained a draft of Trump's Ukraine peace plan — negotiated between the Trump administration and Moscow by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — which would require Ukraine to cede occupied territories to Russia and limit the size of the Ukrainian military. Ukrainian officials described the proposal as decidedly favorable to Russia, which had started the war through an unprovoked invasion. The plan included a side agreement on security guarantees that explicitly did not obligate the US or European allies to intervene in the event of future Russian aggression against Ukraine. Ukrainian officials told Axios that after a five-hour Kremlin meeting between Witkoff, Kushner, and Putin, the US proposal worsened from Kyiv's perspective, with American envoys seemingly selling Russia's demand for full Donbas annexation. Trump gave Zelensky a Thanksgiving deadline to accept the plan. Zelensky said Ukraine faced an impossible choice between national dignity and losing its primary backer. Trump claimed Zelensky's negotiators love the plan while Russian officials simultaneously registered objections.

Trump set a Thanksgiving deadline for Kyiv to respond.

title: Trump Immigration System Held Children in Detention for Months, AP Reports
description_short: Trump Immigration System Held Children in Detention for Months, AP Reports
description_medium: An Associated Press report found that ICE was holding hundreds of children and parents at the Dilley family detention center, many beyond a longstanding 20-day limit. The report followed public concern over a five-year-old detained in Minneapolis and transferred with his father to Texas. Families described prolonged detention and disruption, while experts warned of harm to children.
description_long: When ICE officers in Minneapolis detained a 5-year-old boy and his father last month and sent them to a Texas detention center, many Americans were alarmed. But he was hardly an outlier. ICE has been holding hundreds of children and their parents at the Dilley detention facility, many for well beyond the 20-day limit set by longstanding court order. When Dilley opened in 2014 most families held there had just crossed from Mexico. But since the Trump administration reopened it last spring, the number of children and parents held there has risen sharply. Many are families who have lived in the U.S. for several years, uprooting children in what both families and experts say is often a traumatizing experience. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: Kash Patel Guts FBI Iran Counterintelligence Unit Before U.S. Strikes
description_short: Kash Patel Guts FBI Iran Counterintelligence Unit Before U.S. Strikes
description_medium: CNN reported that FBI Director Kash Patel fired about a dozen members of the bureau’s Iran-focused counterintelligence team days before U.S. strikes in 2026. Sources said the personnel were targeted because of their work on the Mar-a-Lago documents investigation; one specialized in Iranian threats. The firings raised concern about lost informant relationships and weakened Iran expertise.
description_long: In early March 2026, days before the United States launched major military operations in Iran, FBI Director Kash Patel fired approximately a dozen agents and staff members from CI-12, the FBI's Washington D.C.-based counterintelligence squad that handled espionage cases including threats from Iran and its proxies. According to CNN and CBS News reporting on March 3, 2026, the agents were fired specifically because they had worked on the investigation into Trump's alleged retention of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. Among those terminated was a section chief in counterintelligence who specialized in Iranian government threats. A source described the effect as devastating to the FBI's Iran program, noting that the fired agents maintained confidential informants in the Iranian community that could not be replicated by new personnel. The firings stripped the United States of its domestic intelligence capability against Iran at the precise moment the nation was contemplating military escalation with Tehran. The CIA cannot operate domestically, making the FBI's Iran program uniquely critical—and uniquely exposed by Patel's politically motivated purge.

title: Federal Judge Rules Trump Third-Country Deportation Policy Unlawful
description_short: Federal Judge Rules Trump Third-Country Deportation Policy Unlawful
description_medium: A federal judge ruled that the administration’s policy of sending immigrants to countries where they had no ties was unlawful, because people were entitled to notice and a chance to object. Judge Brian Murphy paused the ruling for 15 days to allow an appeal. The dispute followed an earlier Supreme Court order that had let a deportation flight to South Sudan proceed.
description_long: A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration’s latest policy of deporting immigrants to “third countries” to which they have no ties is unlawful and must be set aside. U.S. District Judge Brian E. Murphy in Massachusetts agreed to suspend Wednesday's decision for 15 days, giving the government time to appeal his latest ruling in the case. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the administration’s favor last year, pausing Murphy’s previous decision and clearing the way for a flight carrying several migrants to complete its trip to war-torn South Sudan, where they had no ties. Murphy said migrants challenging the policy have the right to notice and an opportunity to object before they are removed to a third country. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: Hegseth Shares Yemen Strike Plans in Second Signal Chat With Wife and Brother
description_short: Hegseth Shares Yemen Strike Plans in Second Signal Chat With Wife and Brother
description_medium: A CBS News report said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared Yemen strike schedules in a second Signal group chat that included his wife, brother, lawyer, and other non-Cabinet contacts. An aide had reportedly warned him against using an unsecured system. Pentagon officials denied classified material was shared, while the new report raised questions about whether the first Signal incident was isolated.
description_long: On April 20, 2025, the New York Times reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had shared detailed military strike information in a second Signal group chat—this one on his personal phone and including his wife Jennifer, his brother Phil Hegseth (a DHS adviser at the Pentagon), his personal lawyer Tim Parlatore, and approximately ten other non-Cabinet allies. The chat, which Hegseth had originally created during his confirmation process, contained F/A-18 Hornet flight schedules—essentially identical to the classified operational data he had shared in the first Signalgate chat. An aide had explicitly warned Hegseth before the Yemen operation not to share sensitive information on unsecured communications systems. Hegseth continued regardless. Neither Jennifer Hegseth nor brother Phil had any operational need for Yemen strike timelines. The Defense Department's acting inspector general was already investigating the first Signal chat. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell denied any classified material was shared. Thirteen people were in the second chat; the breach demonstrated the first incident was not isolated but reflected systematic disregard for operational security protocols.

title: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Medical Neglect, Deaths at Fort Bliss ICE Camp
description_short: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Medical Neglect, Deaths at Fort Bliss ICE Camp
description_medium: An 84-page Human Rights Watch and ACLU report described assaults, medical neglect, poor conditions, and barriers to contacting lawyers at Camp East Montana, an ICE facility at Fort Bliss. Of 71 detainees interviewed, about 90 percent said they experienced or witnessed assaults. Three people died in the facility’s first months, and a separate GAO report cited serious oversight failures.
description_long: Camp East Montana, a sprawling ICE detention facility opened in August 2025 on Fort Bliss Army base in El Paso, Texas, became the subject of a devastating 84-page joint report by Human Rights Watch and the ACLU released in July 2026. Of 71 detainees interviewed over five months, approximately 90% — 64 individuals — said they had personally been assaulted by staff or witnessed others being beaten. Detainees reported being denied necessary medical care, forced to live in filthy conditions, and fed inedible meals. They were prevented from contacting lawyers or family members. Three detainees died at the facility in little more than six months, including a 55-year-old Cuban migrant who died in January 2026 after being held down by guards — and evidence in that death was missing or destroyed, per a Government Accountability Office report released June 2026. The GAO found significant, pervasive issues with planning, oversight, missing use-of-force reports, failure to administer medicine to seriously ill detainees, and tens of millions in wasted taxpayer funds through rushed contracts.

title: CISA Election Security Team Placed on Leave, Dismantled
description_short: CISA Election Security Team Placed on Leave, Dismantled
description_medium: The Trump administration placed election-security staff at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on leave in February 2025 and later cut more than 130 agency jobs. The changes included regional specialists who worked with state election offices and defunding a nationwide election-threat sharing program. Officials warned the reductions could leave states with less federal support against cyberattacks and foreign influence.
description_long: Beginning February 7, 2025, the Trump administration placed at least 17 staffers from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Election Security and Resilience team on administrative leave, pending a review focused on anti-disinformation activities. Within weeks, more than 130 CISA employees overall were fired, including 10 regional specialists who liaised directly with state and local election offices. Acting CISA director Bridget Bean issued a Valentine's Day memo defunding the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center (EI-ISAC), a nationwide program providing threat monitoring to state election officials. The memo ordered a review of every election security position and program dating back to Trump's first term. Attorney General Pam Bondi on February 5 separately disbanded the FBI task force on election threats against election workers. Democrats on the Senate and House oversight committees warned the moves left states without federal protection against ransomware and foreign cyberattacks ahead of the 2026 midterms. Former officials said the cuts specifically targeted staff who had monitored Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence operations in the 2024 election cycle.

title: DOJ Sues 30+ States Demanding Detailed Voter Registration Databases
description_short: DOJ Sues 30+ States Demanding Detailed Voter Registration Databases
description_medium: The Justice Department sued states that refused to provide detailed voter-registration data, including addresses and partial Social Security numbers. By 2026, the department had filed cases against more than 30 states and D.C.; courts had ruled against its demands in the first 16 decisions. States cited privacy and federalism concerns, while critics warned the data could enable federal surveillance of voters.
description_long: Beginning in mid-2025 and escalating through 2026, the Department of Justice launched an unprecedented campaign to compel all 50 states and the District of Columbia to turn over detailed voter registration databases containing voters' full names, dates of birth, residential addresses, driver's license numbers, and last four digits of Social Security numbers. The DOJ pursued this under a confidential memorandum of understanding framework citing EO 14248. By May 2026, the DOJ had filed lawsuits against 30 states and D.C. that refused. By July 2026, courts had ruled against the DOJ in all 16 federal court decisions issued on the matter, with a Rhode Island judge calling it a fishing expedition and seven of the 15 district court judges who ruled against Trump having been appointed by Trump himself. Even Republican-controlled states including Idaho, Utah, West Virginia, and Kentucky resisted, citing privacy concerns. Critics warned the consolidated database would create a federal surveillance tool over American voters. Democratic states described it as an attempt to nationalize elections in violation of the Constitution's elections clause.

title: LGBTQ Federal Employees Targeted in DEI Purge and Firings
description_short: LGBTQ Federal Employees Targeted in DEI Purge and Firings
description_medium: Trump’s January 2025 orders targeted federal DEI programs and LGBTQ protections in government employment. They placed some employees on leave, restricted employee resource groups, and revoked a longstanding contractor rule that barred discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The Williams Institute estimated hundreds of thousands of federal, postal, and contractor workers could be affected.
description_long: Beginning January 20, 2025, Trump's executive orders on DEI and 'gender ideology' immediately placed employees whose roles involved 'promoting gender ideology' on paid administrative leave with computer access cut off, and at least six EOs directly targeted LGBTQ people in the federal workforce. The Williams Institute estimated approximately 314,000 LGBTQ employees of the federal government, USPS, and federal contractors were exposed to displacement. An OPM memo in early February directed agencies to prohibit employee resource groups promoting 'DEIA initiatives,' and OPM opened a tipline for workers to report colleagues involved in DEI activities — drawing comparisons to the 1950s 'Lavender Scare.' Trump also rescinded a nearly 60-year-old executive order (EO 11246) on January 21, 2025 prohibiting discrimination by federal contractors, removing protections for roughly 100,000 LGBTQ contractor employees. The Department of Homeland Security announced it would allow its agents to conduct surveillance based solely on a target's gender identity or sexual orientation. On March 26, 2025, a class-action complaint was filed before the Merit Systems Protection Board on behalf of fired federal DEI employees.
